title: The Walkman reaches America
what: Sony's pocket stereo cassette player, the TPS-L2, went on sale in the United States in June under the name Soundabout. Abroad it is also sold as the Stowaway in Britain and the Freestyle in Sweden and Australia.
why: The Walkman turns Sony into a global consumer brand; Sony shares more than double in dollars during 1980.
note: Should have a story about de

title: Sony shows a camera without film
what: On 25 August Sony unveiled a prototype of the Mavica, an electronic still camera that records pictures as analog video signals instead of on film. Sony has not said when it might go on sale.
why: An early glimpse of electronic imaging, the field in which Sony's image sensors later dominate.

title: Sony sells the first compact disc player
what: Sony launched the CDP-101, the first compact disc player sold to consumers. The compact disc format was developed jointly by Sony and Philips.
why: The CD becomes the music format of the next two decades and leads Sony into owning a record company. The launch date of 1 October is from data/news/1982.json; the source re-read here confirms only the year.

title: Japan buys America: Sony takes over CBS Records
what: Sony completed its purchase of CBS Records, for 2 billion dollars on 5 January. It is the most visible sign so far of a new pattern: since the Plaza agreement of 1985 the dollar buys only about half as many yen as before, so American companies and buildings have become cheap for Japanese buyers, whose own shares and land stand at record prices. CBS keeps the rights to the CBS name for music recordings and gives Sony a temporary licence to use it.
why: Sony now owns hardware and content; the music business later becomes one of its steadiest earners.

title: Sony buys Columbia Pictures
what: On 28 September Sony obtained an option to buy Coca-Cola's 49% stake in Columbia Pictures Entertainment, as part of a takeover of the whole studio. The next day it agreed to buy Guber-Peters Entertainment for 200 million dollars and hired producers Peter Guber and Jon Peters to run Columbia.
why: The Columbia deal: the biggest Japanese purchase of an American company at the time and a symbol of the bubble years. It ends in a 2.7 billion dollar write-off five years later.
changed: rule on metrics: takeover price per share dropped

title: Tokyo's crash drags Sony down
what: Japanese share prices have collapsed this year: by 30 August the market had fallen to half its December 1989 record, as the Bank of Japan raised its discount rate step by step to 6%. Sony shares fell 22% in dollars in September.
why: Sony is not a bank, but its shares fall with Tokyo. They rebound 23% in October. [Lookahead review: 'peak' implied the final high.]

title: Sony announces it will enter the games console market
what: On 27 October Sony said it is entering the video game console market with a machine called PlayStation, built around 3D graphics. Sony and its Japanese music company have set up Sony Computer Entertainment, led by engineer Ken Kutaragi, to run the business.
why: The PlayStation becomes Sony's most important business for the next three decades.

title: Morita steps down; the Columbia write-off
what: Co-founder Akio Morita, who suffered a cerebral haemorrhage last year, stepped down as chairman on 25 November and was succeeded by Norio Ohga. Sony has also taken a 2.7 billion dollar write-off on its American film studio.
why: The reckoning for the Hollywood purchase. A 1998 report dates the write-off to more than three years before February 1998; the exact announcement month is not confirmed in the sources read.

title: The PlayStation goes on sale in Japan
what: Sony released the PlayStation in Japan on 3 December, a week after Sega's Saturn. Launches in North America and Europe are planned for 1995.
why: The PlayStation: the product that rescues Sony's profits in the late 1990s and builds its games business.

title: PlayStation launches in America and Europe
what: The PlayStation went on sale in North America on 9 September and in Europe on 29 September.
why: The global launch; PlayStation outsells Nintendo and Sega in the generation.

title: The 'Sony shock': a surprise loss and a 30% fall
what: On 24 April Sony reported a net loss of 111 billion yen (about 930 million dollars) for the three months to March, almost three times what some analysts had expected, as sales of televisions and Vaio computers shrank and prices fell. For the year to March 2004 it forecasts a net profit of only 50 billion yen, less than half the 115.5 billion of the year just ended, after about 140 billion yen of restructuring costs. In Tokyo the shares fell the next day by the maximum the exchange allows, about 13%, and by about a quarter within two days; Japanese newspapers speak of the 'Sony shock', and the Nikkei index dropped to its lowest in 20 years. Sony's shares lost 30% in April, while the S&P 500 rose 8%.
why: The moment investors stopped treating Sony as the unassailable leader of consumer electronics; the 20,000 job cuts of October 2003 and the change of chief in 2005 follow from it. The shock also marked the Nikkei's low after the bubble, on 28 April 2003.

title: Sony to cut 20,000 jobs
what: Sony announced it will cut 20,000 jobs, 13% of its workforce, over three years to save about 3 billion dollars a year by 2006, and cut its operating profit forecast by 23%. It leads in plasma televisions but has only about 5% of the fast-growing LCD TV market.
why: The lost decade in one item: Sony is losing the flat-screen race to Samsung and Sharp.

title: Howard Stringer becomes Sony's first foreign chief
what: On 7 March Sony said Howard Stringer, the Welsh-born head of its American business and a former president of CBS, will succeed Nobuyuki Idei as chairman and chief executive in June. He is the first foreigner to run a major Japanese electronics company.
why: Stringer revives films and music but cannot fix electronics.

title: PlayStation 3 launches
what: Sony released the PlayStation 3 in Japan on 11 November and in North America on 17 November; the European launch slips to March. More than 81,000 units sold in Japan in the first 24 hours.
why: An expensive console that loses money for years (about 3.3 billion dollars on hardware by mid-2008).

title: Hackers break into the PlayStation Network
what: Sony learned on 19 April of an intrusion into its PlayStation Network and shut the service down. Personal details from about 77 million accounts were compromised, one of the largest data breaches so far.
why: A reputational low point in a year that also brings the Japanese earthquake and record losses.

title: Kazuo Hirai named chief executive
what: On 1 February Sony said Kazuo Hirai, who ran the PlayStation business, will become president and chief executive on 1 April, succeeding Howard Stringer.
why: Hirai's 'One Sony' turnaround: sell PCs, shrink TVs, bet on games, sensors and entertainment.

title: Sony doubles its loss forecast to 520 billion yen
what: On 10 April Sony said its loss for the year to March will be 520 billion yen, about 6.4 billion dollars, more than twice its February forecast, because of write-offs of deferred tax assets. Its US shares fell 10% that day.
why: The bottom stretch of the lost decade: the ADR falls 22% in April and reaches its low in November 2012.

title: Hedge fund Third Point pushes Sony to split off entertainment
what: On 14 May Dan Loeb's Third Point, which holds more than 6% of Sony, wrote to chief executive Hirai proposing to separate the film and music business from the struggling electronics arm. Sony's shares have risen 96% this year. The ADR gained 23% in May.
why: Activist pressure that Sony resists; it keeps entertainment, which later becomes its strength.

title: Sony sells its Vaio PCs and spins off TVs
what: Sony announced the sale of its Vaio PC division to the investment fund Japan Industrial Partners and will turn its television business into a separate company. The TV business has lost about 7.8 billion dollars over a decade.
why: Hirai cuts the businesses that made Sony famous but no longer earn money.

title: Sony buys Toshiba's image sensor business
what: This year Sony bought Toshiba's image sensor business, strengthening its position as the leading maker of the camera chips used in smartphones.
why: Sensors become one of the pillars of the comeback. The month of the deal is not confirmed in the source.

title: Sony sells its battery business
what: This year Sony sold its lithium-ion battery business, which it pioneered in 1991, to Murata Manufacturing, and closed its landmark Sony Building in Tokyo's Ginza for redevelopment. Sony's ADR rose about 60% during 2017.
why: The comeback year: profits from games, sensors and entertainment, and an exit from commodity hardware.

title: Kenichiro Yoshida succeeds Hirai
what: Kazuo Hirai handed over as chief executive in April and became chairman; his successor is Kenichiro Yoshida, who had led Sony's internet provider So-net and taken it public in 2005.
why: Yoshida continues the shift towards games, music, films and sensors.

title: Sony merges its phone, TV and camera businesses
what: During 2019 Sony merged its mobile phone, television and camera businesses into one unit. Sony's ADR rose about 40% this year.
why: Consolidating the shrinking hardware while games, sensors and music carry the company. The month of the merger is not confirmed in the source, hence a year-end beat.

title: Sony to become Sony Group and buy out its finance arm
what: On 19 May Sony said it will rename itself Sony Group Corporation from April 2021, with the electronics business taking the Sony Corporation name, and will make Sony Financial Holdings, of which it owns about 65%, a wholly owned subsidiary through a takeover bid.
why: The new structure: a holding company over games, music, films, sensors, electronics and finance.

title: Sony becomes Sony Group
what: On 1 April Sony Corporation was renamed Sony Group Corporation, and the electronics business took over the Sony Corporation name. Sony Financial Holdings, bought out last year, is now wholly owned.
why: The holding structure of the comeback years.

title: Sony closes PlayStation studios
what: As part of company-wide layoffs Sony shut down its PlayStation London Studio in May.
why: Cost discipline in games after the post-pandemic boom. [Lookahead review: cut the closures later in 2024.]

title: Sony hands its TV business to a venture led by TCL
what: Sony and the Chinese electronics maker TCL agreed to form a joint venture for televisions, professional displays and home audio. TCL holds 51% and runs development, manufacturing and distribution; Sony keeps 49% and licenses the brand and core technology.
why: The end of Sony as a television maker, the business of the Trinitron.
